title: Ten courses of action
hookLine: why some go to good destinations and some to bad: ten ways of acting

lines: A LIST FOR THE KITCHEN WALL.
cards: The Buddha is wandering in the Kosala country and comes to a village of brahmin householders called Sala.

They've heard about him, and they come with a question: why do some beings, when they die, go to good places, and some to bad? They're not monks; they're householders. So the Buddha doesn't give them a meditation manual.
He gives them a list they could pin to the kitchen wall.

teach.h: WHY GOOD PLACES? BECAUSE OF ACTION
teach.b: In the discourse to the people of Sala, the forty-first of the Middle-Length Sayings, the answer is short: it's because of how they act. Then the Buddha opens it into ten.
Three are done with the body: killing living beings, taking what isn't given, and sexual misconduct.

teach.h: THREE OF BODY, FOUR OF SPEECH
teach.b: Four are done with speech: lying, divisive speech that splits friends apart, harsh speech, and idle chatter, talk that's useless and badly timed.
And three are done with the mind: covetousness, wanting what belongs to someone else; ill will, wishing others harm; and wrong view, the belief that actions have no results at all.
Those ten, he says, lead to unhappy destinations. Then he turns them over. Someone abandons killing and lives with the rod laid down, gentle and kind to all living things.
Abandons stealing. Is faithful. Speaks the truth.
Speaks to bring people together. Speaks gently, words pleasant to the ear and going to the heart. Speaks at the right time, about what matters.
Doesn't covet. Wishes others well. Sees that actions have results.
Those ten lead to happy destinations. Notice the proportions: four of the ten are about speech, more room than anything else on the list.

teach.h: THREE OF MIND, WHERE NO ONE SEES
teach.b: And three happen only in the mind, where no one else can see.

teach.h: TURN THEM OVER: TEN WHOLESOME WAYS
teach.b: So the list reaches all the way in: what you do, what you say, and what you quietly wish.
Later Buddhist teachers still teach these ten, sometimes as the ten wholesome deeds: a whole ethics that fits on one wall.

how: The ten wholesome and unwholesome courses of action (dasa kusala kammapatha) are taught in Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana settings as a basic guide to ethical life, sometimes to lay people alongside the five precepts.

o: a road of pilgrimage between ten shrines
ten tasks a king set for his ministers
ten courses of action, in body, speech, mind

games.q: sort the ten — tap the pairs.

s: the ten courses are only about outward actions
three of the ten happen only in the mind: covetousness, ill will and wrong view.
speech gets more courses than body or mind
four of the ten are about speech: lying, divisive, harsh and idle talk.
the Buddha gave this teaching to a gathering of monks
he gave it to the brahmin householders of the village of Sala.

games.q: you're a householder of Sala. you ask the Buddha why some beings go to good places after death and some to bad. what does he say first?
o: it's because of how they act.
games.why: his short answer is: because of conduct. then he opens it into ten courses of action, of body, speech and mind.

practice: Go through the good ten slowly in your mind: gentle with living things, honest with what's mine, faithful, truthful, uniting, gentle in speech, saying what matters, content, wishing well, trusting that actions count.
Let the one today could use stand out, and if any ill will is sitting there, let it soften toward wishing well.

wordCard.voice: kammapatha. Three of body, four of speech, three of mind: the ten ways, wholesome or not, that the Buddha told the people of Sala shape where a life goes.

orig.note: Pali kammapatha: a course or path of action. dasa kusala kammapatha: the ten wholesome courses.

carryVoice: Your line: ten courses. What you quietly wish is on the list too. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 41, Saleyyaka Sutta (the discourse to the people of Sala)
